title: The Web Could Have Been Closed
paragraphs: It is easy to forget that the World Wide Web could have turned out very differently. Many early networked systems were controlled by a single organisation, and the Web could easily have followed that pattern. This essay looks at why that did not happen. Tim Berners-Lee wrote his first proposal for a distributed information system at CERN in March nineteen eighty nine, resubmitted a lightly edited version in May nineteen ninety, and by the end of that year had a working server and browser. Nothing about that early success guaranteed that the technology would become a shared public resource.

The turning point came on thirty April nineteen ninety three, when CERN's directors signed a statement placing the Web software in the public domain. Anyone could now use, copy and build on the code without asking permission or paying a fee. The next version of the software in nineteen ninety four moved to an open source licence, which preserved that freedom in a more formal way. That single statement of permission removed a barrier that might otherwise have lasted for years.

Why does the decision still matter? Because openness lowered the cost of experimenting: anyone with a computer could publish a page without seeking approval from a gatekeeper. A closed system might still have succeeded commercially, but it would probably have grown more slowly and reached fewer people. Openness did not guarantee quality, and the Web has since filled with both brilliant and worthless pages. Even so, the freedom to publish remains its defining feature.
